items.prompt: What does MVP stand for in startup terminology?

options.label: Minimum verified plan
Maximum value proposition
Minimum viable product
Main validated purchase

rubric: An MVP is the minimum viable product, the simplest version that can test an idea with real customers.
Other options are invented phrases that sound plausible.

items.prompt: What is the term for the specific group of people a business aims to serve first?

options.label: Market regulator
Board of advisors
Supplier network
Target customer

rubric: The target customer is the specific group the business is built to serve.
Suppliers, advisors and regulators are other parties, not the customers.

items.prompt: In a business model, what do 'revenue streams' describe?

options.label: The places where goods are stored
The people who work in the business
The tools used to make the product
The ways the business earns money

rubric: Revenue streams are the ways a business earns money from customers.
Distractors confuse revenue with staff, resources or logistics.

items.prompt: What is it called when founders fund a new venture mainly with their own savings and early sales?

options.label: Crowdlending
Bootstrapping
Franchising
Venture capital

rubric: Bootstrapping means self-funding with personal money and early revenue.
Venture capital and crowdlending rely on outside investors or lenders.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a customer discovery interview?

options.label: To ask the customer to invest money in the business
To close a first sale with the customer right away
To announce the launch date and collect sign-ups
To learn about the customer's real problems

rubric: Discovery interviews are for learning about customers' problems and needs.
Selling or fundraising turns the conversation into a pitch instead of learning.

items.prompt: Which of these are common sources of early funding for a new venture? Select all that apply.

options.label: Competitors' profits
Angel investors
Customer pre-orders
Government tax audits
Personal savings

rubric: Savings, angel investors and pre-orders are all recognised early funding sources.
Competitors' profits and tax audits are not funding sources a founder can draw on.

items.prompt: Sam has an idea for a meal-prep service. Before cooking anything, he builds a one-page website describing the service with a 'Sign up' button, then counts how many visitors click it. What is this kind of quick test usually called?

options.label: A break-even audit
A supplier contract
A landing page test
A patent filing

rubric: A landing page test measures interest before building the product.
Patent filings, audits and contracts are different activities that do not measure demand.

items.prompt: Why should founders talk to potential customers before building the product?

options.label: It removes the need to compete with others
It guarantees that investors will fund the idea
It lets them skip writing a business model
It confirms the problem is real before money is spent

rubric: Talking to customers early checks the problem exists before resources are spent.
Distractors promise guarantees or shortcuts that customer talks cannot provide.

items.prompt: A software founder charges customers 10 dollars every month for access to her tool. Which revenue model is this?

options.label: Licensing
Subscription
Advertising
One-time sale

rubric: Recurring fees for ongoing access are a subscription model.
A one-time sale charges once; advertising and licensing earn money differently.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains a value proposition?

options.label: The legal form the company registers under, such as a sole trader or a limited company
The reason a customer would choose your offer over alternatives
The total amount of money the founder wants to raise from investors in the first round
The list of tasks the team must finish each week to launch the first version

rubric: A value proposition states the benefit that makes customers choose you.
Other options describe funding, task planning or legal structure.

items.prompt: A new bakery spends more each month than it earns and has no other funding. What is most likely to happen eventually?

options.label: It will run out of cash and be unable to operate
Costs will shrink by themselves as the bakery gets established
Customers will accept higher prices once the bakery has been open a while
Sales will rise as word spreads about the bakery's low profits

rubric: Spending more than earning without funding drains cash until the business cannot operate.
Distractors assume costs, prices or sales will correct themselves automatically.

items.prompt: Why is a customer paying a deposit stronger evidence of demand than a customer saying 'I would buy that' in a survey?

options.label: Survey answers are anonymous, so they cannot be traced to real buyers
Paying costs the customer something, so it shows real commitment
A deposit proves the product works, so further testing is unnecessary
Deposits come from larger samples, so they are statistically more reliable

rubric: Paying shows real commitment, while saying yes is cheap and often over-optimistic.
Distractors make absolute claims that are untrue.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why early customers matter to a new venture? Select all that apply.

options.label: They remove the need to keep tracking costs
They prove people will actually pay for the offer
They make a business plan unnecessary forever
They give feedback that shows what to improve
They can recommend the product to others

rubric: Early customers give feedback, prove willingness to pay and can spread word of mouth.
Customers do not remove the need to track costs or to plan.

items.prompt: Lena launches a budgeting app free of charge and gets 500 downloads in a month, but none of the users upgrade to the paid plan. She wonders what this result suggests about her idea.

options.label: The paid plan must be too cheap for customers to notice
Lena should stop talking to users and just add more features
People may like trying it but not yet value it enough to pay
The idea is certainly a success because downloads are high

rubric: Downloads show interest, but no upgrades suggest the value is not yet worth paying for.
Treating downloads as success ignores the lack of payment, and adding features without feedback is guesswork.

items.prompt: Why do founders usually interview potential customers before building a product?

options.label: To confirm the problem is real and painful enough that people would pay to solve it
To collect compliments that show the idea is good before any money is spent on design
To learn which features competitors offer so that every one of them can be copied
To get friends to promise they will buy once the finished product is ready to ship

rubric: Interviews test whether a real, costly problem exists before building anything.
Distractors treat politeness, promises or copying as validation, which are weak evidence.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a minimum viable product (MVP)?

options.label: A low-cost, rough product released widely so that early sales alone show whether it works
A polished prototype demonstrated to investors to secure funding before any customer sees it
A full-featured product built to completion so the first customers get the complete offer
The simplest version that lets you test your core assumption with real customers

rubric: An MVP is the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption with real users.
Distractors confuse it with sloppy work, a finished product or an investor demo.

items.prompt: A gym charges each member $30 every month for unlimited access. Which revenue model is this?

options.label: One-time sale
Commission
Subscription
Freemium

rubric: Recurring fixed payments for ongoing access is a subscription.
Freemium would give a free tier; commission takes a cut of transactions.

items.prompt: Which description is the best example of a well-defined customer segment for a new invoicing tool?

options.label: Small businesses of all kinds in any country that want to grow
Remote freelance designers who invoice several clients every month
Anyone who owns a smartphone and sometimes pays or sends money
People aged 18 to 65 who may need some kind of financial software

rubric: A good segment is specific, identifiable and shares one recurring need.
Distractors are so broad that no single message or channel could reach them.

items.prompt: What does it mean to bootstrap a new venture?

options.label: Funding it from your own savings and early revenue without outside investors
Selling shares to venture capital firms in exchange for a large first cheque
Raising donations from the public through a crowdfunding page before launch
Borrowing the full start-up cost from a bank before making any first sale

rubric: Bootstrapping relies on personal funds and revenue the business earns.
Distractors describe outside funding such as equity, loans or crowdfunding.

items.prompt: Which of the following are signs of real demand during early validation? Select all that apply.

options.label: A prospect introduces you to a colleague who has the same problem
Friends tell you at dinner that your idea sounds great
Your launch post collects many likes from people you know
A prospect pays a deposit to pre-order before the product exists

rubric: Payment and referrals are costly actions that signal genuine need.
Compliments and likes cost nothing and are weak evidence.

items.prompt: A baker interviews 10 locals about gluten-free sourdough. Eight say they would love it, but when she offers samples to buy at $6, nobody buys. What does this result best show?

options.label: The price is certainly the only problem, so she should halve it and relaunch at once
Interviews are useless for validation because customers always lie about their wishes
Stated interest is weaker evidence than buying behaviour, so demand is still unproven
Ten people is too few, so the interview answers should be ignored completely

rubric: What people say is weaker than what they pay for; demand remains unproven.
Distractors jump to one cause or discard the evidence rather than testing further.

items.prompt: A product sells for $25 with a variable cost of $10 per unit. Fixed costs are $1,500 per month. How many units must be sold each month to break even?
rubric: Break-even = 1,500 / (25 - 10) = 100 units.
Distractors come from dividing by price (60), by cost (150) or by the wrong sum (43).

items.prompt: A founder spends $600 on ads in a month and gains 30 new paying customers from them. What is the customer acquisition cost (CAC)?
rubric: CAC = ad spend / new customers = 600 / 30 = $20.
Distractors subtract, invert the ratio or use an unrelated figure.

items.prompt: You think students will pay for a weekly meal-prep service. Which first test is cheapest and most direct?

options.label: Build an app with ordering and delivery tracking, then ask students to try it
Offer three set meals for pre-order to 20 students and count the paid orders
Survey 200 students on whether they like the idea of meal prep services
Rent a commercial kitchen for a month and cook before anyone has ordered

rubric: A small paid pre-order tests willingness to pay at low cost.
Other options spend heavily first or rely on opinions rather than purchases.

items.prompt: A freelance bookkeeper wants her first clients and serves dental practices. Which approach is the best way to find early customers?

options.label: Build a general website and wait for it to rank in search results over the coming months
Post daily on social media about bookkeeping tips and hope that dentists notice the page
Email and call 30 local offices personally and offer a free first month
Run a regional TV advertising campaign aimed at all small local businesses in the area

rubric: Direct outreach to a narrow, reachable segment is the fastest early-customer route.
Distractors are broad, slow or passive and don't reach the named segment.

items.prompt: Materials and labour cost $12 per unit. You want a 40% margin, meaning profit is 40% of the selling price. What price should you set?
rubric: Price = 12 / (1 - 0.40) = $20, so profit is $8, which is 40% of the price.
$16.80 and $19.20 mix up markup and margin; $24 doubles cost.

items.prompt: A founder will test a landing page for a pet-sitting service. Which are good success criteria to set before the test starts? Select all that apply.

options.label: Collect as many likes and shares as possible on launch day
At least 10 of 40 interviewed owners agree to a paid pilot
At least 5% of 400 visitors join the waitlist within 14 days
The page feels like it is getting plenty of interest from visitors

rubric: Good criteria are specific, measurable and tied to a commitment.
Vague feelings and likes can't tell you whether the idea passed or failed.

items.prompt: A web designer has $5,000 in savings and a client ready to sign. She needs a $3,000 laptop and software to start an agency. She wants to keep full ownership. Which funding choice fits best?

options.label: Bootstrap with her savings and ask the client for a deposit upfront
Take a large bank loan to cover the laptop plus a year of office rent
Pitch venture capital firms for $500,000 in exchange for a large equity share
Give a friend 20% of the business in return for the $3,000 she needs

rubric: The need is small and she has savings and a client, so bootstrapping keeps ownership.
Other options add debt, give up equity or raise far more than the need.

items.prompt: A subscription costs $40 per month with a 70% gross margin. Customers stay 10 months on average, and acquiring one costs $250. What is the LTV:CAC ratio, using gross-margin lifetime value?
rubric: Distractor 1.60 uses revenue instead of margin; 0.89 inverts the ratio.

items.prompt: A product sells for $25 and has $10 variable cost per unit. Fixed costs are $3,000 per month. How many units must be sold per month to break even?
rubric: Contribution per unit is 15, so 3,000 / 15 = 200 units.
Distractors divide by price only (120), by variable cost only (300), or by price plus variable cost (86).

items.prompt: Unit cost is $12. The founder wants a 40% gross margin measured on the selling price. What price should she set?
rubric: $16.80 and $18.00 confuse margin with markup on cost; $24 uses a 50% margin.

items.prompt: A startup has $90,000 in the bank, monthly revenue of $10,000 and monthly expenses of $25,000. Assuming nothing changes, how long is its runway?

options.label: 3.6 months
6 months
9 months
4.5 months

rubric: Distractors use gross expenses only (3.6) or revenue only (9).

items.prompt: A founder interviewed 8 gym owners who all described the same scheduling pain. She has no product yet. Which next step best applies the validate-before-build approach?

options.label: Register the company and trademark the brand so the idea is protected before testing
Survey 200 gym members on whether they like the idea of online class booking
Run a manual pilot for three gyms for a small fee and track whether they renew
Hire a developer to build the full booking platform so gyms can see it working first

rubric: A paid manual pilot tests willingness to pay and continued use cheaply before building.
Building first or surveying opinions skips behavioural evidence from the actual buyers.

items.prompt: A founder wants to test demand for a new meal-prep service before investing in a kitchen. Which tests give real evidence of demand? Select all that apply.

options.label: Publish a landing page with a price and a pre-order button, then count purchases
Ask friends whether they would buy and count the enthusiastic replies
Collect refundable deposits from interested buyers before production starts
Deliver the service by hand to five paying customers as a concierge version
Build the complete app with every planned feature before showing it to anyone

rubric: Concierge delivery, priced pre-orders and deposits all measure actual payment behaviour at low cost.
Building everything first and asking friends are costly or biased and do not show willingness to pay.

items.prompt: A founder built a simple appointment-reminder tool for dental clinics. She has 40 clinic contacts from a previous job and a $500 budget. She wants her first 10 paying customers within two months. Which approach best applies early-customer tactics?

options.label: Email one well-written announcement to all 40 contacts and follow up only with those who reply
Spend the $500 on social media ads aimed at small businesses across her country to build awareness
Build a press kit and pitch dental trade media first so clinics start contacting her themselves
Call each contact, offer a discounted pilot, and ask happy clinics for referrals

rubric: Early customers usually come from direct, personal outreach to a known niche, with referrals extending it.
Broad ads, passive waiting and a generic email do not use her existing warm contacts effectively.

items.prompt: A landing page got 2,000 visitors and 60 free-trial sign-ups (3%), but none of the 60 converted to paid after the trial. What is the most likely explanation to test first?

options.label: The 3% sign-up rate is too small a sample to mean anything, so the test should be repeated with 20,000 visitors before drawing any conclusion
The product lacks features, so the next step is to build the most requested ones and then rerun the same free trial for a new cohort
Free sign-ups measured curiosity, not willingness to pay, so demand was weaker than it looked
Trial users typically churn at the end of any free period, so zero paid conversions is within normal range and the offer needs no change

rubric: Free sign-ups are a weak proxy; zero paid conversions suggests no proven willingness to pay.
Distractors blame sample size, normalise churn or assume features without diagnosing the signal.

items.prompt: In customer interviews a founder asks, 'If I built an app that tracks your freelance invoices, would you use it?' Nearly everyone says yes. What is the main flaw in this evidence?

options.label: It asks about hypothetical future behaviour, so answers reflect politeness, not what people do today
The question names a specific feature, and feedback on features is more reliable when collected through a written survey than in a conversation
The sample is too small, since interviews need at least 100 participants before the answers can be treated as valid evidence
Yes answers are only reliable once the founder has built a working prototype to show people during the interview

rubric: Hypothetical, leading questions produce unreliable answers; past behaviour is stronger evidence.
Sample size and survey format are not the core flaw; a prototype is not required for good interviews.

items.prompt: A model charges $5 per month per user. The only channel is in-person sales visits costing about $300 per customer acquired, and users stay about 8 months. Which part of the business model conflicts most with another?

options.label: Channel cost versus revenue: $300 to acquire a customer worth about $40 in lifetime revenue
Customer segment versus value proposition: a $5 price implies the product has no real value
Revenue streams versus customer relationships: subscriptions cannot coexist with personal sales
Key resources versus cost structure: in-person visits always require a large office

rubric: Lifetime revenue of about $40 cannot repay a $300 acquisition cost, so channel and revenue conflict.
Other distractors invent conflicts that do not follow from the numbers.

items.prompt: A founder is choosing between a bank loan with fixed monthly repayments and equity from an angel investor. Revenue is expected to be near zero for 12 months. Why is the loan the riskier fit here?

options.label: Loans always carry higher interest than the return an equity investor expects, so they cost more overall
Loans must be repaid in one lump sum at the end of year one, which is impossible with no revenue
Banks take control of company decisions, which stops founders from changing product direction
Repayments are due whatever the sales, so zero revenue turns the schedule into a cash drain that can force closure

rubric: Fixed repayments continue regardless of revenue, creating cash-flow risk during the pre-revenue period.
Distractors state false generalisations about interest, bank control and lump-sum repayment.

items.prompt: Monthly revenue has grown 20% for six months. Cohort data shows only 10% of each month's new customers are still paying after month 2. What does this pattern show?

options.label: Growth is healthy because revenue is rising, and retention becomes a priority once the company reaches profitability
Growth comes from new customers replacing heavy churn, so it will stall if acquisition spending slows
Retention is low because the price is too low, so raising prices should improve churn in most cohorts
Cohort data is unreliable at this size, so revenue growth is the more trustworthy metric to track for now

rubric: Rising revenue can hide a leaky bucket; poor cohort retention means growth depends on continuous acquisition.
Other options dismiss retention or assume a price fix without evidence.

items.prompt: A founder reviews interview notes. Which findings suggest the problem is genuinely urgent rather than merely polite interest? Select all that apply.

options.label: The interviewee said the idea was 'great' and promised to tell friends
The interviewee already pays for a clumsy workaround to handle the task
The interviewee asked when they could start paying for a solution
The interviewee agreed that the problem sounds common in the industry
The interviewee described the last time the problem occurred and what it cost them

rubric: Paid workarounds, concrete recent costly episodes and unprompted purchase requests show real urgency.
Praise, promises to tell friends and agreeing the problem is common are cheap signals.

items.prompt: A founder sells weekly meal boxes. Her first 30 customers came from friends, family and her gym. After that network was exhausted, she spent $900 on ads and gained 4 customers. She concludes the product is the problem. Which analysis best explains the data?

options.label: Four ad customers from $900 show the market is too small to support the business, so she should pivot to a new product before spending more on acquisition
Friends' purchases are biased and invalid data, so the first 30 sales say nothing about product quality and she must restart validation with strangers only
Early sales came from personal trust, so they never showed a repeatable channel; the ad result tests the channel, not the product
Ads rarely work for perishable food products, so she should drop paid channels for good and rely only on word-of-mouth from her existing customers

rubric: Network sales do not show a scalable channel; poor ad results point to channel fit, not necessarily product failure.
Distractors over-generalise from one small ad test or discard the early data entirely.

items.prompt: A founder ran 30 customer interviews for a scheduling app. 25 people said the idea was 'great' and 'they would definitely use it', but none agreed to a paid pilot or a follow-up call. What is the most likely explanation for this pattern?

options.label: The interviews collected polite opinions, not evidence of commitment, so real demand for the problem is still unproven
The sample of 30 is too small, so the enthusiasm can't be trusted until at least 300 people are interviewed
The app's price was too low, which made interviewees doubt the product's quality and decline pilots
The interviewees were the wrong age group, so positive opinions would have turned into pilots with younger people

rubric: Compliments without commitment (money, time, introductions) are weak evidence; the signal is the refusal to commit.
Sample size and demographic explanations ignore that enthusiasm without action is the core flaw.

items.prompt: A startup sells a $40/month subscription. Customer acquisition cost is $120, gross margin is 70%, and average customers cancel after 4 months. Which analysis of the unit economics is correct?

options.label: Each customer yields about $112 gross profit, so the model works once the founder raises the acquisition budget
Each customer yields $28 monthly profit, which covers the $120 cost after 3 months, so payback occurs before churn
Each customer yields $160 revenue, above the $120 acquisition cost, so each acquisition is profitable
Each customer yields about $112 gross profit over its life, below the $120 acquisition cost, so each acquisition loses money

rubric: 40 x 4 x 0.7 = $112, less than $120 CAC.
Using revenue instead of gross profit, or miscounting payback (120/28 is about 4.3 months), hides the loss.

items.prompt: A founder's landing-page test got 2,000 visitors and 6% signed up for the waitlist. Visitors came from a viral post about a free tool. Only 1% of the waitlist later replied to a paid-offer email. What does this comparison best show?

options.label: The free-tool traffic inflated sign-ups, so the 6% overstated demand from buyers
The paid-offer email was badly written, so the 1% reply rate says nothing about demand from paying customers at all
The 6% sign-up rate proves the market is large, and the drop to 1% is a normal funnel step the founder can ignore
The waitlist was too small to support any conclusion, so the founder should wait for many more sign-ups before acting

rubric: Audience quality matters: free-seeking traffic inflates top-funnel metrics.
Dismissing the drop as normal or blaming only the email ignores the mismatch between the audience and a paying customer.

items.prompt: A meal-kit founder finds that 70% of revenue comes from customers reached by one partnership with a gym chain, while paid ads bring almost no repeat buyers. Which risk does this breakdown most clearly expose?

options.label: Weak brand awareness in general, which only more ad spend can fix
Underpricing across the catalogue, since the gym customers accept the current prices without complaint
Dependence on a single channel, so losing the gym partnership could erase most revenue
Overspending on product development, since ads fail to convert customers who are repeat buyers

rubric: Revenue concentration in one channel is a fragility risk.
Pricing, awareness, and product spend aren't what the data isolates.

items.prompt: Two founders both interviewed 20 restaurant owners about a food-waste tracker. Founder A asked 'Would you use a tool that tracks waste?' Founder B asked 'Tell me about the last time you threw out a lot of food.' Why is B's approach more reliable for validating the problem?

options.label: It avoids mentioning the product, which guarantees that owners give longer, more detailed answers
It produces more quotable stories, which makes investor presentations more persuasive
It elicits specific past behaviour, which is harder to exaggerate than hypothetical intentions
It lets owners vent about their suppliers, which gives the founder the pricing data needed

rubric: Past behaviour is stronger evidence than hypothetical statements.
Other options mistake side effects (length, venting, quotes) for the validity benefit.

items.prompt: A founder of a B2B invoicing tool sees that trial sign-ups are rising but paid conversions are flat for three months. Which of the following analyses would help isolate the cause? Select all that apply.

options.label: Count total social media followers over the same three months
Compare conversion rates by acquisition channel to see whether newer channels bring weaker-fit users
Interview trial users who didn't convert about what they used instead
Review whether trial users reach the first successful invoice, to find onboarding drop-off

rubric: Channel segmentation, activation analysis and lost-user interviews each isolate a cause of flat conversion.
Follower counts are a vanity metric unrelated to conversion cause.

items.prompt: A founder built a pet-sitting marketplace. After six months, 400 sitters signed up but only 30 owners booked, and most sitters never got a job. The founder spent most of the budget recruiting sitters because supply 'must come first'. Which diagnosis best explains the stall?

options.label: Owners distrust online marketplaces in general, so the model can't work however supply is managed, and any further spending on growth would be wasted
The sitter sign-up form was too long, which filtered out good sitters and is why the number of owner bookings stayed low
Sitter supply outran owner demand, so most sitters saw no jobs and are likely to leave, which lowers bookings further
The platform needs more sitters still, since only 30 bookings show that owners find the choice of sitters too limited

rubric: Marketplace imbalance: oversupply with thin demand leaves sitters idle and churning.
Adding more supply worsens the imbalance; the form and general distrust claims lack support.

items.prompt: A founder has $60,000 in savings and must pick one funding route for a niche software tool with slow, steady growth potential and a founder who wants to keep control. Criteria: keep control, keep dilution minimal, tolerate slow growth. Which route fits best?

options.label: Take a high-interest short-term loan, since debt never affects control or cash flow
Raise a large venture round, since it provides the most capital and the growth expectation is easy to adjust later
Bootstrap with early customer revenue, since it preserves control and matches the slow-growth profile
Pursue equity crowdfunding from thousands of backers, since it keeps ownership concentrated in the founder

rubric: Bootstrapping matches the control and slow-growth criteria.
Venture capital imposes growth expectations and dilution; crowdfunding adds owners; high-interest debt strains cash flow.

items.prompt: A founder must choose a first customer segment. Criteria: reachable with no ad budget, urgent problem, ability to pay within 30 days. Option fits: (a) hobbyists, easy to reach, low urgency; (b) small dental clinics, reachable via local associations, urgent billing delays, own budgets; (c) large banks, urgent but 9-month purchasing cycles; (d) students, large group, little money. Which is best?

options.label: Students, because a large group offsets low spending and ensures fast payment
Large banks, because their urgent need and deep budgets outweigh the slow purchasing cycle
Small dental clinics, because they meet reachability, urgency and payment-speed criteria together
Hobbyists, because easy reach matters more than urgency or ability to pay

rubric: Only the clinics satisfy all three stated criteria.
Banks fail the 30-day payment criterion; hobbyists and students fail urgency or ability to pay.

items.prompt: A founder has a prototype and can either spend three months building the full product or run a two-week concierge test, delivering the service manually to five paying customers. The main uncertainty is whether customers will pay. Which is the better judgement?

options.label: Run the concierge test, since it tests willingness to pay at far lower cost before building
Run the concierge test, since five paying customers is enough to prove the product will scale nationally
Build the full product, since customers cannot judge a manual service and so will not pay for it until it is automated
Build the full product, since a manual test teaches nothing about how customers use software and so cannot guide the build

rubric: The riskiest assumption is payment; a cheap manual test addresses it first.
The last option correctly picks the test but overclaims what five customers prove.

items.prompt: A founder weighs two pricing plans for a design tool: $15/month with an expected 400 customers, or $45/month with an expected 120 customers needing sales calls. Support capacity is limited to 150 customers, and the founder has no time for sales calls. Which plan best fits these constraints?

options.label: Neither, since any price will break the support capacity
The $45 plan, since it earns more per customer, though the time for sales calls is unavailable
The $15 plan, since the higher volume gives more revenue and the support limit can be ignored
The $15 plan, since 400 customers exceeds the support limit and the calls are infeasible, making it unworkable

rubric: $45 x 120 = $5,400 vs $15 x 400 = $6,000, but 400 customers exceeds the 150 support cap; the $45 plan stays within the cap.
The first option is tempting but the sales-call constraint is the weaker one to resolve; the key follows the support cap and the premium revenue per customer.

items.prompt: A founder wants to judge whether an early traction metric shows product-market fit. Which evidence is the strongest, given the criterion that it must reflect customers who value the product without heavy persuasion?

options.label: A rising count of downloads in the weeks after a large paid advertising campaign
A high number of press mentions and social shares after the launch announcement
Enthusiastic positive comments from friends and family who tried the first version
Strong week-over-week retention among users who found the product organically

rubric: Organic retention shows ongoing value without push.
Downloads, press, and friends' comments reflect promotion or goodwill rather than sustained need.

items.prompt: A founder judges a proposal to give a large discount to the first 10 customers in exchange for case studies. The criteria: learn real willingness to pay, gain credible proof, protect margins. Which concerns are valid points for critiquing the proposal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Heavy discounts may anchor customers on a low price that is hard to raise later
Customers paying a steep discount reveal little about what they would pay at full price
Case studies from heavily discounted early adopters may persuade fewer buyers who pay full price
Discounting to early customers always lowers the founder's chance of getting any referrals later

rubric: Anchoring, weaker pricing signal, and explicit exchange of value are real considerations.
Case studies are widely used in sales, so the claim that they never help is false.

items.prompt: A founder has 8 weeks of runway left and two plans. Plan A: polish the product for a big launch in week 8. Plan B: contact 40 target customers each week, selling the current rough version for a paid pilot. Criteria: learn from real payments, extend runway, limit the risk of running out of cash unnoticed. Which plan is better supported?

options.label: Plan A, since a polished product gives cleaner feedback on demand, and a launch in week 8 still leaves time to adjust before cash runs out
Plan B, since weekly paid pilots bring in cash and evidence early, while Plan A risks all runway on an untested launch
Plan A, since a polished launch draws more press and attention, and early sales of a rough version could hurt the brand with first customers
Plan B, since pilot revenue will cover costs once a few customers pay, so the founder can stop tracking weekly cash and focus on selling

rubric: Plan B meets all three criteria: payments, runway extension, early signal.
The last option picks Plan B but wrongly assumes revenue is guaranteed.

items.prompt: A founder interviewed 30 prospective customers about a new scheduling tool. 24 said they would definitely buy it, but none has been asked for money. Judged on strength of evidence, which assessment is best?

options.label: Strong evidence, provided the 30 interviewees were drawn from the intended target segment
Weak evidence: the sample is too small, so run 300 more interviews before concluding
Weak evidence: intent is cheap, so ask for deposits or signed pilots and count only those
Strong evidence: 24 of 30 is an 80% positive rate, well above normal validation thresholds

rubric: Stated intent costs nothing; commitment such as deposits or pilots is the stronger signal.
Distractors treat a high positive rate or sample size as the main issue, missing the lack of real commitment.

items.prompt: A founder plans niche compliance software with a realistic market ceiling of about $15M annual revenue, 70% gross margins, and a wish to keep control. Judged against these criteria, which funding approach fits best?

options.label: Use paid pilots and revenue, since a market this size cannot return venture-scale outcomes
Rely on crowdfunding alone, because it is the only route that avoids owing anyone anything
Raise a large venture round, because outside capital speeds growth in every software market
Take a bank loan for the full product build, because debt never dilutes control or adds risk

rubric: A small, profitable niche suits revenue-funded growth; venture investors need outcomes this market cannot provide.
Distractors assume capital is always good, or that debt or crowdfunding is risk-free.

items.prompt: A founder prices an inventory-planning tool at cost plus 30%, which is $200 a month. The tool typically saves customers about $5,000 a month. Which critique of this pricing is strongest?

options.label: Cost-plus ignores value delivered; test prices anchored to the $5,000 monthly savings
The price is too high; it should stay near cost so the product wins market share quickly
The markup is too low against a 50% industry norm, so raise it to exactly that level
Price should match the lowest competitor listing, since buyers compare only on price

rubric: Cost-plus ignores the value customers capture, so it leaves large revenue unclaimed.
Distractors replace one cost- or competitor-based rule with another instead of anchoring to value.

items.prompt: A pet-meal subscription founder lists four assumptions. The criterion is to test first the one that would sink the business if false and is cheapest to test. Which assumption should be tested first?

options.label: Customers will refer friends, which only a year of subscriber data can really show
A cheaper packaging supplier exists, which a handful of quotes can check next quarter
A well-known vet will endorse the brand, which cold emails may reveal over months
Customers will pay $60 a week, which a pre-order page can test within days

rubric: Willingness to pay is fatal if false and cheap to test quickly.
Other options are either low-impact or slow and costly to test.

items.prompt: After 9 months and 6 product iterations, a SaaS startup has steady sign-ups, but only 8% of users are still active after 30 days, flat across every cohort and every iteration. Judged on this evidence, what is the best decision?

options.label: Persevere and double ad spend, since steady sign-ups prove the market for it exists
Wait another quarter, since retention figures are meaningless before a full year
Treat flat retention as weak core value and test a different problem or segment
Add more features, since flat retention means the product lacks needed functions

rubric: Retention that does not move despite repeated iteration suggests the core value or segment is wrong.
Distractors mistake acquisition for demand or assume more of the same effort will change flat retention.

items.prompt: A pitch sizes its market as: 'The global pet industry is $200B; capturing just 1% gives us $2B.' Which are valid criticisms of this reasoning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Market size should always be stated in units sold rather than in revenue
It lacks bottom-up logic linking price, customers reached and conversion rates
It never identifies a reachable segment or how many buyers the product can actually serve
A 1% share is too low to be credible for any startup in any market
Total industry size says nothing about whether this product meets an unmet need

rubric: Top-down 'just 1%' sizing ignores reachable segment, bottom-up logic and actual need.
Distractors invent rules about share size or units that are not valid criticisms.

items.prompt: A two-person startup sells workflow software to dental clinics. One clinic chain provides 70% of revenue and demands a custom integration that would take two months of the only developer's time, or it will leave. Criteria: survive, and keep building a product other clinics will buy. What is the best response?

options.label: Build it exactly as the chain specified, since losing 70% of revenue would end the company
Offer a generalised version funded by a paid commitment, after checking other clinics want it
Refuse politely, since any custom work inevitably destroys the focus of a small product team
Build it free as a goodwill gesture, which will lock in the chain's loyalty for several years

rubric: A paid, generalised build protects revenue while keeping the roadmap useful to the wider segment.
Distractors either surrender the roadmap to one customer or ignore the survival risk.

items.prompt: A founder with $500 and two weeks must test whether freelance designers will pay $29 a month for an invoicing tool that is not yet built. Which design meets all the constraints and shows real payment behaviour?

options.label: Build the full tool on no-code first, then see whether anyone signs up after launch
Survey 200 designers on whether they would pay $29, then average the stated answers
Ask in designer forums for feedback on the idea and count the positive comments
Run a priced checkout page for designers with a preset threshold, refunding all orders

rubric: A priced checkout with a preset threshold tests real payment behaviour within budget and time.
Distractors measure opinion or need more time and money than the constraints allow.

items.prompt: A founder has $40,000 and wants to launch a $120 smart water bottle. The factory demands a 5,000-unit minimum costing $150,000. Which plan meets both constraints: limited cash and no big unsold inventory?

options.label: Borrow for the full 5,000 units, because unit cost falls sharply at that volume
Make 500 units at another cheap factory without testing quality or customer demand
Order 5,000 units on factory credit and clear unsold stock at steep discounts later
Take pre-orders using a prototype, then fund a small first batch from the deposits

rubric: Pre-orders turn demand into cash that funds a small first batch and limits inventory risk.
Distractors take on large inventory risk or skip validation of quality and demand.

items.prompt: A B2B startup sells to about 200 logistics firms, has no ad budget, and needs its first 5 paying customers within 90 days. Which acquisition plan meets these constraints?

options.label: Run a viral consumer social campaign and hope logistics buyers happen to notice it
Hire commissioned sellers and let them each define their own target lists freely
Founder-led outreach to the named 200 firms with a paid pilot offer, logging objections
Publish a weekly blog and wait for search traffic to build up over the next year

rubric: A small, named market and a paid pilot make direct founder outreach the fastest, cheapest route.
Distractors are slow, untargeted, or rely on spending and delegation the startup lacks.

items.prompt: A founder builds a marketplace for home tutors. Parents won't join without tutors and tutors won't join without parents. Constraints: no subsidy budget, one city, three months. Which design best resolves the cold start?

options.label: Pay both sides large sign-up bonuses for instant liquidity, funded by later rounds
Launch nationally with a broad feature set so both sides quickly find enough value
Pick one subject and area, recruit tutors personally, and hand-match parents
Wait for a funded rival to prove the model, then copy its app feature for feature

rubric: Narrowing to one niche and hand-matching builds density without subsidies.
Distractors spread thin, delay action, or require funding the founder lacks.

items.prompt: A plan to scale paid ads reasons: CAC is $120, average revenue is $20 a month, monthly churn is 10%, so lifetime revenue is $200, well above CAC. The product's gross margin is 40%. What is the plan missing?

options.label: A larger ad budget, since scale will lower CAC whatever the churn rate turns out to be
Margin-adjusted value: at 40% margin lifetime profit is about $80, below the $120 CAC
A longer horizon, since lifetime value should only be counted after the first three years
A competitor price check, since price alone decides whether a given CAC is acceptable

rubric: Lifetime value must use gross profit: $200 x 40% = $80, below the $120 CAC.
Distractors ignore margin and assume scale or horizon fixes the economics.

items.prompt: A founder must design a 6-week test of whether small restaurants will pay for a food-waste tracking service. Constraints: the result must support a clear go or no-go decision, and only one test can be run. Which elements should the plan include? Select all that apply.

options.label: One narrowly defined restaurant segment so results can be interpreted
Testing three prices and four segments at once to maximise learning
Payment or signed commitment as the measured behaviour, not survey opinions
Success and kill thresholds written down before the test starts
Counting any positive reply as a conversion to reach the threshold faster

rubric: Preset thresholds, real commitment and a narrow segment make one test decision-grade.
Distractors dilute the sample or inflate results, which breaks interpretability.

items.prompt: A founder has 6 months of runway, a prototype and 3 pilot users. Constraints: reach evidence for a seed raise (paying customers and repeat usage), hire no one, and keep 2 months of cash in reserve. Which plan fits all the constraints?

options.label: Convert pilots to paid, sign 10 buyers in one segment, track repeat use, cap spend at 4 months
Hire two engineers now to speed up the roadmap, so investors see a bigger team and a faster build pace
Spend four months building a full v2 with the features pilots asked for, then use the last two months to find customers and investors
Pause product work and pitch many seed investors at once, using the vision, a market-size model and pilot quotes

rubric: It produces paying and repeat-use evidence, avoids hiring, and keeps the 2-month cash reserve.
Distractors delay evidence, break the no-hire or reserve constraint, or pitch without traction.
